title: KNN & Naive Bayes
summary: Two simple, still-asked baselines — instance-based K-Nearest Neighbors and probabilistic Naive Bayes — and when each is the right tool.

slides.markdown:
**KNN** and **Naive Bayes** couldn't be more different in spirit — KNN does no learning at all, just remembers the data and looks at what's nearby; Naive Bayes makes a bold, technically-false assumption and predicts anyway.

Both are cheap, easy to reason about, and still show up as fast baselines — KNN for recommendation-style similarity problems, Naive Bayes for text classification like spam filtering.

slides.subTitle: Lazy learning and distance
slides.markdown:
KNN does no training at all — it just stores every training example. At prediction time, it finds the `k` stored points **closest** to the new point (typically by Euclidean distance) and predicts by majority vote (classification) or average (regression).

This is called **lazy learning**: all the work happens at prediction time, not training time. That makes training instant but prediction expensive — every query scans (or indexes) the entire stored dataset.

slides.subTitle: Choosing k
slides.markdown:
`k` is a direct bias-variance dial:

- **Small `k`** (e.g. 1) — the prediction follows the single nearest point exactly, tracing every quirk of the training data. Low bias, high variance — sensitive to noise and outliers.
- **Large `k`** — the vote averages over many neighbors, smoothing out noise but also smoothing over real local structure. Higher bias, lower variance.

A very large `k` can wash out a genuinely local pattern; `k=1` can make one mislabeled neighbor flip a prediction. Tune `k` via cross-validation, and prefer odd values for binary classification to avoid ties.

slides.subTitle: Where KNN struggles
slides.markdown:
**The mistake:** feeding KNN raw, unscaled features, or applying it to hundreds of features expecting the usual accuracy.

**Why it breaks:** distance sums across all features, so one feature on a 0-100,000 scale silently dominates one on a 0-1 scale unless both are standardized first. Separately, in high dimensions points spread out until "nearest" neighbors are nearly as far as random ones — the **curse of dimensionality** erodes what "close" even means.

**The fix:** always scale features before distance, and reduce dimensionality once feature count climbs into the hundreds.

slides.subTitle: The independence assumption
slides.markdown:
Naive Bayes classifies by Bayes' theorem: `P(class | features) ∝ P(class) × P(features | class)`. Computing `P(features | class)` exactly would need to model every feature interaction — infeasible with many features.

The "naive" part: it **assumes every feature is conditionally independent given the class**, so `P(features | class)` collapses into a simple product `P(f1|class) × P(f2|class) × ...`. That assumption is almost always literally false — words in a sentence aren't independent — but it makes the math trivial and the model needs only per-feature statistics.

slides.subTitle: Why it still works
slides.markdown:
Despite the false assumption, Naive Bayes often classifies well — it only needs the **ranking** of class scores right, not their exact values.

Even when features are correlated, ignoring that correlation often biases every class's score in a similar direction, so the *relative order* — the only thing that matters for picking the winner — usually survives. That's why it performs well on spam filtering and document classification, where words are technically correlated but each still carries real class-specific signal.

Instance-based vs probabilistic — different assumptions, different failure modes.

| | KNN | Naive Bayes |
|---|---|---|
| Learns | Nothing (stores data) | Per-feature probabilities |
| Prediction cost | High (searches all points) | Very fast (lookup + multiply) |
| Needs scaling | Yes | No |
| Shines on | Small, dense, numeric data | High-dimensional, sparse (text) |

Reach for KNN on small numeric datasets where similarity is meaningful; reach for Naive Bayes on high-dimensional sparse data like text, where it's fast and hard to beat as a baseline.
